title: The Reading Room and the Seventy-Eight Cards: Waite, the Auditor of Secret Traditions
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Brooklyn, the birth of Arthur Edward Waite
stops.date_confidence: attested full date (Wikipedia, Britannica); no street or parish recorded, coordinate is the borough centroid
stops.campa: On the second of October a son is born in Brooklyn to Charles Frederick Waite, an American sea captain, and Emma Lovell, an Englishwoman out of a London merchant family. No street is recorded and no parish; the borough is the whole of what the record keeps. The boy will spend his life among documents that name their places exactly, cataloguing Rosicrucian charters and lodge minutes and the dates of first editions. The first document of his own life gives a city on the far side of an ocean he will cross once, as an infant, and never cross again.
stops.quote: In conclusion as to this part, I will give these further indications regarding the Fool, which is the most speaking of all the symbols. He signifies the journey outward, the state of the first emanation, the graces and passivity of the spirit. His wallet is inscribed with dim signs, to shew that many sub-conscious memories are stored up in the soul.
stops.quote_source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910), Part II, section 3, 'Conclusion as to the Greater Keys'
suggested_refs: Brooklyn birth records for October 1857, not located in this session
sources: controverscial.com, biography of A. E. Waite

stops.name: The North Atlantic, the death of Captain Waite
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Wikipedia); exact day 29 September 1858 rests on controverscial.com alone; the coordinate is an open-ocean placeholder, no position is recorded anywhere
stops.campa: Somewhere on the trans-Atlantic run the captain dies at sea, his son not yet a year old. Nothing the biographies quote gives a log or a port of report; the ocean takes the fact and keeps the position. The pin here is open water chosen for the shipping lane rather than a researched location, and it is the one stop in this journey that stands over nothing. Everything that follows proceeds from the vacancy: England, Rome, the Reading Room, the Golden Dawn, and a widow with two small children and no husband's income.
suggested_refs: Lloyd's List and American shipping registers for autumn 1858, not consulted
sources: controverscial.com, biography of A. E. Waite

stops.name: North-west London, the widow's suburbs
stops.date_confidence: return to England attested for 1858 (Wikipedia); the settlement district rests on controverscial.com alone and no street is named; date defaulted to the first of the year
stops.campa: Emma Lovell brings Arthur and his sister Frederika back to England and finds her own family closed against her, scandalised that the children were born before the marriage. Support is withdrawn. She settles with them in what her son's biographer calls the poorer and less fashionable suburbs of north and west London, and takes her children into the Roman Catholic Church. The boy is raised inside a ceremony his mother cannot afford to travel to see performed anywhere grander. He will keep the ceremony long after he stops keeping the faith.
suggested_refs: London parish registers of Catholic conversions, 1858-1863, not consulted
sources: controverscial.com, biography of A. E. Waite

stops.name: Bayswater, two terms at St Charles' College
stops.date_confidence: attendance for two terms around age thirteen attested (Wikipedia), which gives no location; Bayswater comes from controverscial.com, and contradicts the later St Charles Square, North Kensington campus often plotted instead; month and day unrecorded
stops.campa: At thirteen he is sent to a Roman Catholic boys' college for two terms, the whole of his formal secondary education. Latin, catechism, the shape of the liturgical year, and then the money runs out and the schooling stops. What he takes from it is not doctrine but a grammar of a particular kind: the conviction that a rite is a text whose parts can be dated and whose borrowings can be traced to the page they came from. Thirty years on he will read the Golden Dawn's ceremonies exactly that way and find them younger than their claims.
suggested_refs: St Charles' College registers, Bayswater and North Kensington, not consulted
sources: controverscial.com, biography of A. E. Waite

stops.name: London, the death of Frederika
stops.date_confidence: death in 1874 attested (Wikipedia, controverscial.com); month, day and family address all unrecorded, the coordinate is a placeholder
stops.campa: His sister dies. The family address at that date is recorded nowhere, and the pin here stands in for a house that nobody has located. What is recorded is the consequence: the boy of sixteen turns to the question of whether the dead survive, and to the seance rooms and the psychical researchers who claim to answer it. His biographer adds that the death also turned him away from Rome. Waite himself never wrote that sentence down, and it belongs to the biographer rather than to him.
suggested_refs: English death registrations for Frederika Waite, 1874, not searched
sources: controverscial.com, biography of A. E. Waite

segments.name: The Reading Room Under the Dome

stops.name: British Museum Reading Room, an education without a university
stops.date_confidence: attested that regular study begins at about twenty-one (Wikipedia); no month or day, defaulted to the first of the year
stops.campa: At about twenty-one he begins to read daily under the dome in Great Russell Street. He has no degree and will never take one; the Reading Room is his entire higher education and its catalogue is his faculty. He works through alchemy, Kabbalah, Freemasonry, the Rosicrucian pamphlets and the Church Fathers, and he acquires the habit that will make him unbearable to occultists for the next fifty years. He checks the edition and the date, and then whether the manuscript a tradition cites has ever existed.
stops.quote: It seems rather of necessity than predilection in the sense of apologia that I should put on record in the first place a plain statement of my personal position, as one who for many years of literary life has been, subject to his spiritual and other limitations, an exponent of the higher mystic schools.
stops.quote_source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910), Preface
suggested_refs: British Museum Reading Room admission ledgers for 1878, not consulted

stops.name: British Museum Reading Room, the finding of Eliphas Levi
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Wikipedia); month and day unrecorded, defaulted to the first of the year
stops.campa: In the same reading room he opens Eliphas Levi, and the direction of his life is settled. The Frenchman's ceremonial magic is, by Waite's own later measure, unreliable, theatrical and impossible to verify. It is also impossible to put down. He will translate Levi into English, digest him, correct him, and go on quarrelling with him in print for four decades. The verdict he finally arrives at is neither a dismissal nor an endorsement, and in fifty years of revising his opinions he never revises that one.
stops.quote: a brilliant and profound illumine whom it is impossible to accept, and with whom it is even more impossible to dispense
stops.quote_source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910), Part I, on Eliphas Levi (the accented spelling of the original is flattened here)
suggested_refs: The British Museum Library's Levi holdings as catalogued in 1881
sources: Wikisource, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot, Part I

stops.name: George Redway's list, The Real History of the Rosicrucians
stops.date_confidence: publication year attested by the first-edition record; month and day unrecorded; Redway's shop address was not established, so the coordinate is a publishing-district placeholder
stops.campa: George Redway publishes him: first the Levi digest and the poems of Israfel in 1886, then a history of the Rosicrucians that sets out to strip the brotherhood of everything the nineteenth century has draped over it. Bulwer-Lytton's Zanoni had given England an immortal adept living in a Venetian palazzo. Waite goes back to the Fama and the Confessio and reports what those documents will and will not carry. The Christian Rosenkreuz of the pamphlets survives the audit as a figure of literature. The adept of the novels does not.
suggested_refs: The Real History of the Rosicrucians, George Redway, London, 1887, first edition

stops.name: London, the marriage to Ada Lakeman
stops.date_confidence: contradiction left standing: Wikipedia gives 1888, controverscial.com gives 1883 or 1884; no month, day or church recorded by either, and the coordinate is a placeholder
stops.campa: He marries Ada Lakeman and calls her Lucasta, after Lovelace's lady, for the rest of her life and of his. The two principal accounts of his life put the wedding five years apart, and neither shows its working; the church is named in neither. A man who spent his career establishing the exact year of obscure pamphlets left the year of his own marriage in dispute, and the dispute stands here rather than being quietly settled in favour of the tidier source. The same season Redway prints his Lives of Alchemystical Philosophers.
suggested_refs: English marriage registrations for Ada Lakeman, 1883-1888, not searched
sources: controverscial.com, biography of A. E. Waite
Internet Archive catalogue, Lives of Alchemystical Philosophers (Redway, 1888)

stops.name: Holland Park, the house at 17 Lansdowne Road
stops.date_confidence: address and Besant's conversion dates attested in blavatsky.journey.json and annie_besant.journey.json; Waite's presence is not attested and not claimed, this is a contextual pin on the same city
stops.campa: Two years before Waite is initiated, and four miles west of the Reading Room, Helena Blavatsky keeps house at 17 Lansdowne Road, and Annie Besant comes in May to be convinced. London in these years holds several esoteric capitals at once and they do not much visit each other: Theosophy in Holland Park with India behind it, the Golden Dawn in a hired hall with the Rosicrucians behind it, the Societas Rosicruciana in the City with the lodges behind it. Waite will end up inside two of the three and reviewing the third.
suggested_refs: 17 Lansdowne Road, Holland Park, Theosophical headquarters of 1889

stops.name: Dulwich, initiation into the Outer Order
stops.date_confidence: initiation in January 1891 attested (Wikipedia); the venue is contested, controverscial.com places it at Mathers' house Stent Lodge in Dulwich while standard Golden Dawn practice put initiations in a temple hall, and the contradiction is not resolved here
stops.campa: In January he is initiated into the Outer Order of the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn, the body Westcott, Woodman and Mathers had raised out of the decoded Cipher Manuscripts and hung, through the Societas Rosicruciana, on the Gold und Rosenkreuz and on Christian Rosenkreuz himself. He takes the grade as a man who has already read the sources. He knows what the Fama says and what the vault of seven sides is quoting, and he joins anyway, because the ceremony works on him whether or not its pedigree holds.
suggested_refs: Golden Dawn Isis-Urania membership rolls for January 1891, not consulted
sources: controverscial.com, biography of A. E. Waite

stops.name: Isis-Urania, Philosophus and the withdrawal of 1893
stops.date_confidence: grade progression and the 1893 withdrawal attested (Wikipedia); the temple's premises in these specific years are not confirmed, the coordinate follows the usual Mark Masons' Hall attribution and is a reconstruction
stops.campa: He advances to Philosophus by the spring of 1892, and in 1893 he resigns. The order's business is magic of the operative kind: talismans, evocation, skrying, the will worked upon the world. Waite wants the mystical kind, the soul's ascent, and holds that the rest is machinery dressed as religion. He goes out. Three years later he comes back in, and in 1899 he is admitted to the Second Order after all. The quarrel he leaves over is the quarrel he will spend the next twenty years conducting from inside.
suggested_refs: Mark Masons' Hall, 33 Golden Square, Soho, and the other halls that housed Isis-Urania
sources: Wikipedia, 'Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn'

stops.name: London, the alchemists Englished
stops.date_confidence: the Edward Kelly volume is attested for 1893 (Wikipedia bibliography); the Boehme life is carried from jacob_boehme.journey.json and was not confirmed against a catalogue here; month is a placeholder, and the pin is a publishing-district placeholder
stops.campa: He turns translator and editor at scale. The alchemical writings of Edward Kelly go into English, and a life of Jacob Boehme, whose Behmenist line England had received through William Law's edition and had been quietly rereading ever since. The following year he brings out the Hermetic and Alchemical Writings of Paracelsus in two volumes, which will still be the working English text a century later, cited three times over in this atlas's own Paracelsus file. He treats them as authors with something still to say, and puts their sentences into the language one at a time.
suggested_refs: The Hermetic and Alchemical Writings of Paracelsus, 2 vols., London, 1894

stops.name: London, the editorship of The Unknown World
stops.date_confidence: journal run of 1894-1895 rests on the standard Waite bibliography; no office address is recorded, the coordinate is a district placeholder, month and day defaulted
stops.campa: For two years he edits a journal of his own, The Unknown World, a magazine of comparative mysticism that gives him a platform as editor rather than only as author. It runs from 1894 to 1895 and then it stops. The office address is not recorded and the pin here is a guess at a district. The journal fixes the position he will hold for the rest of his life: the mystics of every tradition are describing one interior country, and the magicians, whatever else they are doing, are not describing it.
suggested_refs: Complete run of The Unknown World, 1894-1895
sources: Standard Waite bibliography for the journal run

stops.name: London, Devil-Worship in France and the Levi translation
stops.date_confidence: both 1896 publications attested (Wikipedia bibliography; Internet Archive catalogue for the Redway translation, which corrects a widespread 1910 dating); month and day unrecorded; publishing-district placeholder coordinate
stops.campa: Leo Taxil has spent twelve years selling France an invented Satanic Freemasonry, with a fictitious priestess and forged rites, and Waite writes a book taking the fabrication apart before Taxil confesses the hoax himself. The same year Redway prints his translation of Levi's Dogme et Rituel as Transcendental Magic, the version through which the English-speaking world will read Levi for a century. He rejoins the Golden Dawn in the same season. The exposure and the translation belong to the same year.
stops.quote: The deception and self-deception regarding their origin in Egypt, India or China put a lying spirit into the mouths of the first expositors.
stops.quote_source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910), Part I
suggested_refs: Transcendental Magic, its Doctrine and Ritual, trans. A. E. Waite, George Redway, London, 1896
sources: Internet Archive catalogue record, Transcendental Magic (Redway, 1896)

stops.name: Isis-Urania, the Second Order
stops.date_confidence: admission to the Second Order attested for 1899 (Wikipedia); month and day unrecorded; the premises for that year are unconfirmed and the coordinate is a reconstruction
stops.campa: Admitted at last to the Second Order, he stands inside the Adeptus Minor ceremony, in the vault of seven sides that stages the opening of Christian Rosenkreuz's tomb as the Fama describes it. He has published the audit of that document. He knows the vault is a nineteenth-century carpentry job quoting a seventeenth-century pamphlet, and he stands in it as a man stands in a cathedral he has himself dated to the fifteenth century and not to the first. The year before he had published The Book of Black Magic and of Pacts.
stops.quote: it is the presentation of universal ideas by means of universal types, and it is in the combination of these types, if anywhere, that it presents Secret Doctrine
stops.quote_source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910), Part II, section 1
suggested_refs: The Adeptus Minor ritual and the vault of the Adepti, Isis-Urania Temple

stops.name: Wraysbury, initiation at Runymede Lodge
stops.date_confidence: the year 1901 is attested (Wikipedia); the exact day, the lodge name and its number rest on controverscial.com alone, and the meeting hall is not identified in any source, so the pin stands over the village
stops.campa: On the nineteenth of September he is initiated a Freemason in Runymede Lodge No. 2430, in a village on the Thames. He is forty-three, and he has been writing about the Craft's secret tradition for years without holding a single degree in it. From here the Masonic career runs in parallel with the occult one and outlasts it: lodge, chapter, rite, encyclopedia. The hall where the lodge met is nowhere named in the sources, only the lodge and its number, so this pin stands over the village and not over a door.
suggested_refs: Minute books of Runymede Lodge No. 2430, not consulted
sources: controverscial.com, biography of A. E. Waite

stops.name: Marylebone, raised Master Mason
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the date and the lodge come from controverscial.com alone and are corroborated by nothing else reachable; precision without corroboration is carried here as reconstruction
stops.campa: Five months later he is raised to the third degree at St Marylebone Lodge No. 1305, and the whole of what is known about that day comes from a single popular biography that nothing else corroborates. Precision without corroboration is still a reconstruction and is carried as one here. What the year certainly gives him is standing. The man who writes about Masonic ritual is now a Master Mason, and the standing objection that he writes from outside the tyled door is closed for good.
suggested_refs: Minute books of St Marylebone Lodge No. 1305, not consulted
sources: controverscial.com, biography of A. E. Waite

stops.name: Aldermanbury, admission to the Societas Rosicruciana in Anglia
stops.date_confidence: SRIA membership in 1902 attested (Wikipedia); April comes from controverscial.com alone; the coordinate is the SRIA founding pin inherited byte-identical from bulwer_lytton.journey.json and christian_rosenkreuz.journey.json; day defaulted
stops.campa: In April he is admitted to the Societas Rosicruciana in Anglia, founded in this City street on the first of June 1867 out of Masonic antiquarianism and the Rosicrucian appetite that Bulwer-Lytton's Zanoni had fed. The SRIA is the quarry the Golden Dawn's grade ladder was cut from. In the same year, at the same address, Westcott hands Theodor Reuss a Swedenborgian Rite charter, and the line that will run to the Ordo Templi Orientis leaves London through a door Waite has only just walked in by.
suggested_refs: SRIA membership rolls for 1902, not consulted
sources: controverscial.com, biography of A. E. Waite

stops.name: Freemasons' Hall, exalted in the Royal Arch
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from controverscial.com alone for the date; the coordinate is Freemasons' Hall, Great Queen Street, to within about forty metres; the pool's merging of this event with the SRIA admission a month earlier is undone here
stops.campa: On the first of May he is exalted in the Royal Arch at Great Queen Street, the degree that completes the Craft and hands the candidate a lost word recovered from a vault beneath a ruined temple. He has now been let into three chambers built on one architecture: the Fama's tomb, the Golden Dawn's vault of seven sides, the Arch's crypt. He treats the repetition as evidence rather than as coincidence. The rites are quoting one another, and the quotation is what he means by the secret tradition.
suggested_refs: Royal Arch chapter records at Freemasons' Hall, Great Queen Street, not consulted
sources: controverscial.com, biography of A. E. Waite

stops.name: London, the Theosophical Congress of July 1902
stops.date_confidence: Steiner's July 1902 London visit with Besant present is attested in steiner.journey.json; Waite's attendance is not claimed by any source, this is a contextual pin on the same month and city; day defaulted
stops.campa: Rudolf Steiner crosses from Berlin in July for the Theosophical Congress, with Annie Besant presiding over a movement that now runs from Adyar to Holland Park. Waite is two months into the Societas Rosicruciana and a year away from breaking the Golden Dawn in two. The two men are in one city, working the same seam, and no record shows either noticing the other. Steiner will build a movement on the Rosicrucian name. Waite will spend the decade establishing what that name can and cannot bear.
suggested_refs: Proceedings of the 1902 Theosophical Congress, London

stops.name: Geneva, the Rectified Scottish Rite
stops.date_confidence: the Swiss journey and the rite are attested for 1903 (Wikipedia), which gives the country and no city; Geneva is a plotted guess and is labelled as one; month and day unrecorded
stops.campa: After the Golden Dawn splits he keeps the Isis-Urania name for his own Independent and Rectified Order, and crosses to Switzerland to take the Rectified Scottish Rite, the Christian and chivalric Masonic system of Jean-Baptiste Willermoz. No source consulted names the Swiss city; the country is the whole of the record, and Geneva stands here as a guess plainly labelled. What he brings back is a warrant: a lineage that is documented, Christian and not magical, which is exactly the order he now intends to run.
suggested_refs: Rectified Scottish Rite transmission records for 1903, city unidentified

stops.name: Bibliotheque de l'Arsenal, the French manuscripts
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: recurring use across the 1890s and 1900s is inferred from citations in Waite's own prefaces, no travel diary is known and no individual trip is dated; the date shown is a placeholder inside the range
stops.campa: His Levi, his Martinism and his Kabbalah studies rest on French manuscript holdings, and the Arsenal in Paris is where a good deal of that material sits: the alchemical and illuminist collections that the eighteenth century assembled and the nineteenth catalogued. Individual trips are undocumented. No travel diary is known, and these visits are inferred from the citations in his own prefaces rather than from any record of a crossing. The pattern of use is attested. The journeys themselves are not.
suggested_refs: Bibliotheque de l'Arsenal reader registers for the 1890s and 1900s, not consulted
sources: Inferred from source citations in Waite's published Levi translations and Kabbalah studies

stops.name: Paris, the city of Mathers and Papus
stops.date_confidence: Guenon's entry into Papus's Martinist circle from 1905 is attested in rene_guenon.journey.json; Mathers' Paris relocation and Waite's engagement with the same French material are reconstruction; day and month defaulted
stops.campa: Mathers has moved the Golden Dawn's operative centre to Paris and runs the Ahathoor Temple there, and Papus runs the Martinist Order out of the same city. From 1905 a young Rene Guenon walks into it and begins the reading that will end in a wholesale rejection of the lot. Waite's French is the working kind, and his Saint-Martin biography of 1901 draws on the same well. Two men are auditing the Western occult revival from opposite banks of the Channel, and both conclude that most of its pedigrees are forged.
suggested_refs: The Life of Louis Claude de Saint-Martin, the Unknown Philosopher, London: Philip Wellby, 1901
sources: Internet Archive catalogue record, The Life of Louis Claude de Saint-Martin (Wellby, 1901)

segments.name: Malted Milk and the Seventy-Eight Cards

stops.name: London, manager for Horlicks
stops.date_confidence: the 1900-1909 employment is attested (Wikipedia); the office address is unrecorded and the coordinate is generic London; Horlicks chose Slough for its factory in 1906 and completed it in 1908, so a London pin may cover only the first half of the tenure
stops.campa: For nine years the historian of the secret tradition earns his living selling malted milk. He manages for Horlicks, the invalid-food and bedtime-drink firm, edits its house magazine, and writes the occult books at night. The office address is nowhere recorded, and the company chose Slough for its new factory in 1906 and finished the build in 1908, so a London pin covers at best the first half of the tenure. The tarot deck the twentieth century will reprint by the million is designed by a man on a manager's salary.
stops.quote: The subject has been in the hands of cartomancists as part of the stock-in-trade of their industry; I do not seek to persuade any one outside my own circles that this is of much or of no consequence; but on the historical and interpretative sides it has not fared better.
stops.quote_source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910), Preface
suggested_refs: Horlicks company records and the run of Horlick's Magazine, not consulted

stops.name: London, The Hidden Church of the Holy Graal
stops.date_confidence: publication year attested (Wikipedia bibliography); month and day unrecorded; the coordinate is generic London, no address is on record
stops.campa: He publishes a study of the Grail that reads the whole cycle as the record of an initiation: the wounded king, the waste land, the question that is not asked, the vessel that is not a relic but a rite. The method shows plainest in this book, the literary history and the mystical claim held in one hand. He is fifty-two. Within the same year he will hand a young illustrator a list of seventy-eight scenes and put the same argument into pictures a person can hold in a pack.
suggested_refs: The Hidden Church of the Holy Graal, London, 1909

stops.name: London, the direction of Pamela Colman Smith
stops.date_confidence: Smith's work is dated April to October 1909 (Wikipedia, 'Pamela Colman Smith'); the working location is recorded nowhere, and the pool's pin at 'Waite's home' was fabricated, so the coordinate here is generic London and claims nothing finer
stops.campa: Between April and October he sets Pamela Colman Smith to work, specifying the symbolism card by card. The innovation is in the minor arcana: where earlier decks printed the pips like playing cards, every one of the fifty-six will now carry a scene with people in it. Where the direction happened is recorded nowhere, not his house, not her studio, and this pin says London and nothing finer. She is paid a flat fee. Her initials go into the corner of every card, and her name goes onto none of the boxes.
stops.quote: He is the spirit in search of experience.
stops.quote_source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910), Part II, section 2, on the Fool
suggested_refs: Pamela Colman Smith's surviving correspondence of 1909

stops.name: 164 Aldersgate Street, William Rider and Son publish the deck
stops.date_confidence: December 1909 publication attested (Wikipedia, 'Rider-Waite Tarot'); day unrecorded; the coordinate is the firm's Aldersgate Street address and corrects a pool pin that sat 850 metres south by St Paul's
stops.campa: In December Rider issues it simply as Tarot Cards, a limited first printing with roses and lilies on the back, sold alongside Waite's booklet The Key to the Tarot. A larger run follows in March on better stock, with the pattern collectors will call cracked mud, and that becomes the standard deck, reprinted through 1920 and then on and off until 1939. Nothing about the printing announces that the twentieth century will learn the word tarot from these seventy-eight pictures.
stops.quote: The true Tarot is symbolism; it speaks no other language and offers no other signs.
stops.quote_source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910), Part I, 'The Veil and its Symbols', section 1
suggested_refs: William Rider and Son, 164 Aldersgate Street, London EC1, publisher's records

stops.name: London, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot
stops.date_confidence: the expanded companion volume is attested for 1911 (Wikipedia), the text itself carrying an 1910 imprint in the digitised edition; month and day unrecorded; generic London coordinate
stops.campa: He expands the booklet into a full companion, with all seventy-eight cards illustrated in black and white and a running argument against nearly everyone who has written on the subject. Court de Gebelin's Egypt is a fabrication. Levi is indispensable and unreliable. The fortune-tellers have had the cards as stock-in-trade and taught the public to read the pictures backwards. He supplies the divinatory meanings anyway, in a final section, with a note that he considers them arbitrary in the highest degree.
stops.quote: The Tarot embodies symbolical presentations of universal ideas, behind which lie all the implicits of the human mind.
stops.quote_source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910), Part II, section 1, 'The Tarot and Secret Tradition'
suggested_refs: The Pictorial Key to the Tarot, digitised at en.wikisource.org
sources: Wikisource, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot

segments.name: The Fellowship of the Rosy Cross

stops.name: Wraysbury, Master of Runymede Lodge
stops.date_confidence: the mastership rests on controverscial.com alone and is reconstruction; the 1911 publication of The Secret Tradition in Freemasonry is attested (Wikipedia bibliography); month and day unrecorded
stops.campa: Nine years after his initiation he takes the chair of the lodge that made him, and the occult author is a lodge Master in a Thames-side village. In the following season he publishes The Secret Tradition in Freemasonry, arguing that the Craft's rituals carry a mystical doctrine older than the guild history the lodges tell about themselves. He is now writing about an institution from inside its senior office, which is the position he had been arguing from for a decade without holding it.
suggested_refs: The Secret Tradition in Freemasonry, London, 1911
sources: controverscial.com, biography of A. E. Waite

stops.name: Isis-Urania premises, the Rite dissolved
stops.date_confidence: attested that Waite closed his Independent and Rectified Rite in 1914 (Wikipedia, 'Isis-Urania Temple'); the pool's added claim that the Golden Dawn itself disbanded that year is false and is deleted; month and day unrecorded, premises unconfirmed
stops.campa: He closes the Independent and Rectified Rite entirely, the ceremonial order he had carried out of the Golden Dawn schism eleven years earlier. The Golden Dawn itself does not end here, whatever the summaries say: Felkin's Stella Matutina and Mathers' Alpha et Omega run on for decades, with American temples already working by this year. What ends is Waite's own experiment in running a magical order whose magic he did not believe in. The war begins the same summer and the membership scatters into it.
suggested_refs: Papers of the Independent and Rectified Rite, 1903-1914
sources: Wikipedia, 'Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn'

stops.name: London, the Fellowship of the Rosy Cross founded
stops.date_confidence: founding in July 1915 attested (Wikipedia; controverscial.com); the venue is unrecorded and the coordinate is generic London; day defaulted; no dissolution date is recorded anywhere reachable
stops.campa: In July he founds the Fellowship of the Rosy Cross, and this time the order is the one he wants: Christian and sacramental, with the operative magic taken out and the ceremony left standing. He writes its rituals himself. The Rosicrucian name he had spent thirty years auditing as a historian he now takes up as a founder, on the ground that the pedigree was never the point and the rite is the point. Where the Fellowship met, and when it stopped, are recorded in nothing reachable.
suggested_refs: Ritual books of the Fellowship of the Rosy Cross, written by Waite

stops.name: Ramsgate, the move to the Kent coast
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction with a live contradiction: controverscial.com gives Ramsgate in 1920, Wikipedia's Bishopsbourne article says he spent most of his later life in that village thirty kilometres west, and Wikipedia's own Waite article records no move; the coordinate is Ramsgate town centre, correcting a pool pin on the town's southern edge
stops.campa: At sixty-two he leaves London for the Kent coast, to write. His biographer says Ramsgate. Wikipedia's article on Bishopsbourne says he spent most of his later life in that village thirty kilometres west, and his own biographical article records no move at all. The two Kents are not reconciled here. Every account agrees on the direction. He goes away from the lodge rooms and the publishers' offices, out to the county where he will be buried and to the books of summary that occupy the last twenty years.

stops.campa: Two volumes of encyclopedia, and three years later The Brotherhood of the Rosy Cross, the mature restatement of the history he had first published in 1887. He is by now the man who tells Freemasonry and Rosicrucianism what their own documents will support. The immortal adept of Bulwer-Lytton's Zanoni, alive in a Venetian palazzo, has been off the table in serious writing for a generation, and Waite is the reason, though the novel goes on outselling every correction he ever published.

stops.campa: An anthroposophical congress meets in London, and among the works shown are abstract paintings by Hilma af Klint, the only public hanging of them in her lifetime. She has been painting to a spiritual instruction for twenty years and telling almost no one. Waite's Fellowship is thirteen years old and still working in the same city. Two projects for making invisible orders visible, one on canvas and one in ritual, run within a few miles of each other, and neither leaves any record of the other.

stops.campa: He is buried in the churchyard of a small Kentish village, in a Grade I church with fourteenth-century wall paintings on its walls and the chancel tomb of Richard Hooker, rector here from 1595 to 1600, standing a few yards from the grave. The man who spent fifty years establishing where documents and rites came from lies under a stone nobody has transcribed, in a churchyard whose most famous monument belongs to another man.

stops.name: Stamford, Connecticut, U.S. Games Systems takes the deck
stops.date_confidence: the 1971 acquisition of American rights and the sequence of titles are attested (Wikipedia, 'Pamela Colman Smith'); month and day unrecorded; the coordinate is the company's Stamford base
stops.campa: The American copyright had lapsed in 1966, twenty-eight years and a renewal after publication, and in 1971 a Connecticut games company acquires the rights and begins printing. It calls the deck The Rider Tarot Deck, then Rider Tarot, then Rider Waite Tarot. The publisher's name stays on it and the designer's name stays on it. The illustrator, who drew all seventy-eight and signed every one of them in the corner, is off the box entirely, and stays off it for most of the next four decades.
stops.quote: The allocation of a fortune-telling aspect to these cards is the story of a prolonged impertinence.

stops.campa: The Delaware Art Museum, with the University of Delaware sponsoring, mounts the first exhibition devoted to Pamela Colman Smith, from September into October, and it travels on to the Princeton University Art Museum in November. From here the scholarship begins to say Waite-Smith, and to ask what a flat fee bought in 1909 and what it did not buy: the copyright, the credit, the name on the box, the century of reprints.

stops.name: London, Magician of Many Parts
stops.date_confidence: publication year attested; the biography itself was not reachable in full text for this file and is quoted here only at second hand through Wikipedia's citation of page 361; month and day unrecorded
stops.campa: R. A. Gilbert publishes the biography that remains the standard account, and the estimate in it is the one that has stuck. Not the tarot, not the orders, but the attempt to write the history of Western occultism as a spiritual tradition in its own right, rather than as failed science or as diseased religion. The man who audited everyone else's pedigree is given one of his own, forty-five years after his death, by a scholar working with the same instrument he used.
stops.quote: Waite's name has survived because he was the first to attempt a systematic study of the history of Western occultism, viewed as a spiritual tradition rather than as aspects of protoscience or as the pathology of religion.

stops.name: Stamford, the Smith-Waite Centennial
stops.date_confidence: the 2009 centennial edition and its reversed name order are attested (Wikipedia, 'Rider-Waite Tarot'); month and day unrecorded; Stamford coordinate as above
stops.campa: A hundred years after Rider's first printing the same Connecticut publisher issues a centennial edition and puts the illustrator's name first: Smith-Waite. Rider drops off the title altogether. Later writers treat the reversal of the word order as an act of restitution. It is the one thing about the deck still available to alter. The artwork itself has not changed a line since December 1909, and the scholarship now says Waite-Smith, or simply the three letters RWS.
suggested_refs: The Smith-Waite Centennial Deck, U.S. Games Systems, 2009
